bindings.label: A 59-year-old female had a 2-year history of difficulty understanding spoken language; she described conversation as sounding like noise or buzzing, especially in crowded areas.
59-year-old right-handed female with 12 years of education and a 5-year history of well-controlled hypertension.

She reported spoken conversation sounded like noise or buzzing, especially in crowded areas; she could not understand spoken questions during the interview but comprehended and responded correctly through lip reading or gestural cues; she struggled to understand television dialogue but could follow foreign movies with Korean subtitles; environmental noises like doorbells and ringing phones were perceived and responded to appropriately; a hearing aid prescribed by an otolaryngology clinic did not improve her comprehension.

One year after symptom onset, she began making errors in simple mathematics and her spoken language comprehension declined significantly, though she could still read and write; her writing style became rough with frequent spelling errors; she occasionally forgot things but it did not impact daily life; she had trouble recalling names of familiar neighbors but recognized them visually; her demeanor and personal relationships remained unaffected.

On examination, she scored 17 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, with specific deficits in calculation, recall, and language; neurological examination was unremarkable except for mild rigidity in the right upper extremity; the Korean version of the Western Aphasia Battery showed fluent spontaneous speech with phonemic paraphasia and mild neurogenic stuttering, severe impairments in comprehension and repetition, and mild impairments in visual confrontational naming and word generation; she could read aloud and understand written words and sentences, and communicate in writing with some literal errors; audiological examination revealed mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with pure-tone thresholds of 30 dB in the left ear and 35 dB in the right ear within the 500-2,000 Hz range, speech audiometry thresholds of 50 dB in the left ear and 60 dB in the right ear, and speech discrimination abilities of 32% at 80 dB in the left ear and 20% at 85 dB in the right ear; brainstem auditory evoked potential responses were normal; she recognized six out of eight nonverbal animal sounds and correctly matched four out of six songs to their written titles; neuropsychological testing showed below-normal performance on the Korean version of the Boston Naming Test, ideomotor praxis, Rey figure-copying test, calculation, finger naming, and the semantic subtest of the controlled oral association word recall test; in a Navon figure task, she recognized only small letters; she had difficulty naming famous people but could describe the occupations of some she could not name; routine laboratory tests showed no evidence of comorbid disease.
